title: Lochs's theorem
intro: In number theory, Lochs's theorem concerns the rate of convergence of the continued fraction expansion of a typical real number. A proof of the theorem was published in 1964 by Gustav Lochs.

title: Locus (mathematics)
intro:
In geometry, a locus (plural: loci; Latin for 'place, location') is a set of all points (commonly, a line, a line segment, a curve or a surface), whose location satisfies or is determined by one or more specified conditions.
The set of the points that satisfy some property is often called the locus of a point satisfying this property.

title: Loewner's torus inequality
intro: In differential geometry, Loewner's torus inequality is an inequality due to Charles Loewner.  It relates the systole and the area of an arbitrary Riemannian metric on the 2-torus.

title: Log sum inequality
intro: The log sum inequality is used for proving theorems in information theory.

title: Logic for Computable Functions
intro: Logic for Computable Functions (LCF) is an interactive automated theorem prover developed at Stanford and Edinburgh by Robin Milner and collaborators in early 1970s, based on the theoretical foundation of logic of computable functions previously proposed by Dana Scott. Work on the LCF system introduced the general-purpose programming language ML to allow users to write theorem-proving tactics, supporting algebraic data types, parametric polymorphism, abstract data types, and exceptions.

title: Logical conjunction
Logical consequence
intro: Logical consequence (also entailment or logical implication) is a fundamental concept in logic which describes the relationship between statements that hold true when one statement logically follows from one or more statements. A valid logical argument is one in which the conclusion is entailed by the premises, because the conclusion is the consequence of the premises.

title: Longest-processing-time-first scheduling
intro: Longest-processing-time-first (LPT) is a greedy algorithm for job scheduling. The input to the algorithm is a set of jobs, each of which has a specific processing-time.

title: Lorden's inequality
intro: In probability theory, Lorden's inequality is a bound for the moments of overshoot for a stopped sum of random variables, first published by Gary Lorden in 1970. Overshoots play a central role in renewal theory.
